title: Setting up a calligraphy workspace
subtitle: Light, surface, tools, and posture for dip-pen work at home
excerpt: A calligraphy workspace needs three things: light that falls from the left (for right-handed writers), a surface that tilts between 45 and 90 degrees for broad-edge work, and a clean, dry space to lay out nibs and ink. Everything else is secondary.
sourceNotes: Edward Johnston, Writing and Illuminating and Lettering (1906), chapter on materials and the working position: detailed description of the writing board, lighting, and pen hold that Johnston established as the modern standard for broad-edge calligraphy.

glossaryTerms.definition: A smooth, firm surface tilted at 45 to 90 degrees from the horizontal, used to support the paper at the correct angle for broad-edge calligraphy. The tilt reduces wrist strain and gives better visual feedback on letter proportions.
A strip of paper or thin board placed under the writing hand to prevent skin oils from contaminating the paper surface and affecting ink adhesion.

content.text: Setting up a home calligraphy workspace is mostly about solving three problems: where the light comes from, how the paper sits, and how the hand rests. Get those right and the nibs, inks, and papers are details. Edward Johnston worked at an angled
supported on his lap and tilted against the table edge, which is still the standard arrangement for broad-edge dip-pen work.

Natural light from a window to the left of the work surface is the best starting point for a right-handed writer. The shadow from the pen falls away from the work rather than across the writing line. If natural light is not available, position an adjustable lamp at the same left-side angle, aiming the beam at the paper rather than at the writer's face. Avoid light directly in front of the board, which creates glare on the paper and makes it harder to read the pen angle.

is any smooth, flat, firm surface that can be tilted. A piece of 9 mm MDF cut to 45 x 60 cm is adequate. Lean it against a stack of books or a box on the table, angled at roughly 45 degrees for Foundational and Italic work, steeper for Copperplate. The tilt takes the wrist out of the bent-backward position that flat desk work requires and gives a more natural arc of hand movement. Tape the paper to the board at the top edge only.

A hard board causes the nib to skid slightly and produces a less fluid stroke than a slightly padded surface. Stick two or three layers of newspaper or a sheet of blotting paper to the board surface, then place the writing paper over them. The slight give allows the nib to slow and respond more precisely to the writing stroke.

is a strip of tracing paper or ordinary copy paper slipped under the writing hand. Skin oils transfer from the hand to the paper during a long writing session and cause ink to bead rather than flow smoothly. The guard keeps the paper surface clean. Johnston describes this as essential when working on parchment or vellum, which are particularly oil-sensitive; on cartridge paper it is useful but not critical.

Keep the ink bottle to the right of the board (or left for left-handed writers) so the pen can be dipped without crossing over the writing surface. A small ceramic tile or pallete well for diluting ink is more stable than a glass jar. Keep a lint-free cloth or kitchen roll within reach for wiping nibs without fumbling. Store nibs individually in a small tray or in a narrow foam strip: nibs stored loose in a tin scratch each other and rust faster.

Hold the pen holder between the index and middle fingers with the thumb supporting from below. The hand rests on the side of the little finger or on the hand guard. The elbow stays close to the body and the whole forearm (not just the wrist) moves to form the letters. This forearm movement is the foundation of Copperplate and Spencerian work; for broad-edge, the arm moves more slowly and the wrist position is more important. Sit with the paper slightly to the right of centre of the body, not directly in front, so the arm can move freely at the correct angle to the writing line.
